title: IV. The Lost Dog
paragraphs: Kolya leaned against the fence with an air of dignity, waiting for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he'd long wanted to meet him. He'd heard a great deal about him from the other boys, but until now he'd always kept up an air of disdainful indifference whenever Alyosha was mentioned, and had even "criticized" what he'd heard about him. But secretly he was dying to make his acquaintance; there was something appealing and attractive in everything he'd been told about Alyosha. So this moment mattered: first of all, he had to show himself at his best, to show his independence. "Or he'll take me for thirteen and treat me like the rest of them. And what are these boys to him anyway? I'll ask him once I know him. It's a pity I'm so short, though. Tuzikov's younger than me, and yet he's half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I'm not good-looking, I know I'm ugly, but I have a clever face. I mustn't talk too freely — if I throw myself at him all at once, he might think — ugh! how awful if he thought—!"

Such were the thoughts racing through Kolya's mind while he did his utmost to look as independent as possible. What distressed him most wasn't so much his "ugly" face as his being so short. On the wall in a corner at home he'd made a pencil mark the year before to record his height, and every two months since then he'd anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he'd grown. But alas, he grew very slowly, and this sometimes drove him nearly to despair. His face, in fact, was by no means "ugly"; on the contrary, it was rather appealing — fair, pale skin, freckled. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often lit up with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones, small, very red, but not very full lips; his nose was small and unmistakably turned up. "I've got a real pug nose, a real pug nose," Kolya used to mutter to himself when he looked in the mirror, and always walked away indignant. "But maybe I don't even have a clever face?" he'd sometimes think, doubtful even of that. But it shouldn't be assumed his mind dwelled on his face and height. On the contrary, however bitter those moments before the mirror, he forgot them quickly, and for a long time, "giving himself over entirely to ideas and to real life," as he put it to himself.

Alyosha came out quickly and hurried up to Kolya. Before he even reached him, Kolya could see he looked delighted. "Can he really be that glad to see me?" Kolya wondered, pleased. We might note here, in passing, that Alyosha's appearance had completely changed since we last saw him. He'd given up the cassock and now wore a well-cut coat, a soft round hat, and had his hair cropped short. All of it suited him very well, and he looked quite handsome. His charming face always had a good-humored look; but there was gentleness and calm in his good humor. To Kolya's surprise, Alyosha came out to him just as he was, without an overcoat — clearly he'd hurried out. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.
"Here you are at last! How anxiously we've been waiting for you!"

"There were reasons, which you'll learn shortly. Anyway, I'm glad to make your acquaintance. I've been hoping for the chance a long time, and have heard a great deal about you," Kolya muttered, a little breathless.
"We'd have met anyway. I've heard a great deal about you too — but you've taken a long time getting here."
"Tell me, how are things?"
"Ilusha is very ill. He's certainly dying."
"How awful! You must admit medicine is a fraud, Karamazov," Kolya cried warmly.

"Ilusha has mentioned you often, very often, even in his sleep, in his delirium, you know. One can see you used to mean a great deal to him ... before the incident ... with the knife.... There's another reason too.... Tell me, is that your dog?"
"Yes, Perezvon."
"Not Zhutchka?" Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. "Is she lost for good?"

"I know you'd all like it to be Zhutchka. I've heard all about it." Kolya smiled mysteriously. "Listen, Karamazov, I'll tell you the whole thing. That's what I came for — that's why I asked you to come out here, to explain the whole episode before we go in," he began animatedly. "You see, Karamazov, Ilusha came into the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is like — a pack of little boys. They started teasing Ilusha right away. I'm two classes above, so of course I only watch from a distance. I saw the boy was weak and small, but he wouldn't give in to them; he fought back. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they only teased him more for it. Worst of all, he was dressed horribly at the time — his trousers were too small for him, and his boots had holes in them. They gave him grief over it, jeered at him. That I can't stand. I stood up for him right away and gave it to them hot. I beat them, but they adore me, you know, Karamazov?" Kolya boasted impulsively. "But I've always had a soft spot for children. I've got two chicks at home in my hands right now — that's what kept me today. So they left off beating Ilusha, and I took him under my wing. I saw the boy was proud, I tell you, the boy was proud — but in the end he became devoted to me like a slave: did my every bidding, obeyed me as if I were God, tried to copy me. Between classes he'd run straight to me, and I'd go around with him. Sundays too. People always laugh when an older boy makes friends with a younger one like that, but that's just prejudice. If it's my own choice, that's enough. I'm teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn't I develop him if I like him? You, Karamazov, have taken up with all these fledglings yourself. I can see you want to influence the younger generation — to develop them, to be useful to them — and I assure you, this trait of your character, which I knew about by hearsay, drew me to you more than anything. But let's get to the point. I noticed a kind of softness, a sentimentality, creeping over the boy, and you know I have an absolute hatred of this soppy sentimentality, I've had it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him too: he was proud, yet slavishly devoted to me, and then suddenly his eyes would flash and he'd refuse to agree with me, argue, fly into a rage. I'd sometimes put forward certain ideas; I could see it wasn't so much that he disagreed with the ideas as that he was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool in the face of his affection. So, in order to train him properly, the tenderer he got, the colder I became. I did it on purpose — that was my plan. My goal was to shape his character, to lick him into form, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you follow me without my spelling it out. Suddenly I noticed that for three days running he was gloomy and downcast, not because of my coldness, but over something else, something more serious. I wondered what the trouble was. I pressed him and found out he'd somehow gotten to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father — this was before his death, of course — and Smerdyakov had taught the poor fool a stupid trick, that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry dogs that snap up anything without chewing it, and then watch what happened. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there's been all this fuss about. The people who owned it never fed it at all, though it barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can't stand it.) So it lunged at the bread, swallowed it, and started to squeal — it turned round and round and ran off, squealing as it went, out of sight. That was Ilusha's own account of it. He confessed it to me, crying bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, 'He ran off squealing' — the sight of it haunted him. I could see he was tormented by remorse. I took it seriously. I decided to teach him a lesson about other things too, while I was at it. So I'll admit I wasn't entirely straight with him — I pretended to be more outraged than I really was. 'You've done a rotten thing,' I said, 'you're a scoundrel. I won't tell on you, of course, but I'll have nothing more to do with you for a while. I'll think it over and let you know through Smurov' — that's the boy who just came with me, he's always ready to do anything for me — 'whether I'll have anything more to do with you in the future, or whether I write you off for good as a scoundrel.' He was tremendously upset. I'll admit I felt I'd gone too far as I was saying it, but there was no helping it — I did what I thought was right at the time. A day or two later, I sent Smurov to tell him I wouldn't speak to him again. That's what we call it when two schoolfellows cut each other off entirely. Privately, I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days, and then, if I saw signs of repentance, hold out my hand to him again. That was my plan. But do you know what happened? He heard Smurov's message, and his eyes flashed. 'Tell Krassotkin from me,' he cried, 'that I'll throw bread with pins in it to every dog there is — every last one!' 'So he's got a bit of a temper on him. We'll have to smoke that out of him.' And I started treating him with contempt; whenever I ran into him I'd turn away or smile sarcastically. And right about then, that business with his father happened. You remember? You have to understand he was already worked up to a fever pitch over what had already happened. The boys, seeing I'd given him up, went after him and taunted him, shouting, 'Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!' And soon there were regular skirmishes with them, which I'm very sorry about now. They seem to have given him one particularly bad beating. One day he flew at all of them as they came out of school. I was standing a few yards off, watching. And I swear, I don't remember laughing — quite the opposite, I felt terribly sorry for him, and in another minute I'd have run over to take his side. But he suddenly met my eyes. I don't know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and struck at my thigh, here, in my right leg. I didn't move. I don't mind admitting I have my nerve sometimes, Karamazov. I simply looked at him with contempt, as if to say, 'This is how you repay all my kindness! Do it again if you like, I'm at your service.' But he didn't stab me again; he broke down, terrified of what he'd done, threw away the knife, burst into tears, and ran off. I didn't rat on him, of course, and I made everyone keep quiet, so it wouldn't reach the masters. I didn't even tell my mother until it had healed. And the wound was barely a scratch. And then I heard that the same day he'd been throwing stones and had bitten your finger — but you understand now what state he was in! Well, it can't be helped: it was stupid of me not to come and forgive him — that is, make peace with him — once he fell ill. I regret it now. But I had a particular reason. So now I've told you the whole thing ... though I'm afraid it was stupid of me."

"Oh, what a shame," Alyosha exclaimed, with feeling, "that I didn't know before what things stood between you two, or I'd have come to you long ago to beg you to come with me to see him. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in his delirium. I had no idea how much you meant to him! And you really haven't managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been hunting all over town for it. Would you believe it, since he's been ill I've heard him say, three times, with tears, 'It's because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I'm sick now. God is punishing me for it.' He can't get the idea out of his head. And if the dog were found and turned out to be alive, one might almost imagine the joy of it would cure him. We've all pinned our hopes on you."
"Tell me, what made you hope I'd be the one to find him?" Kolya asked, intensely curious. "Why did you count on me rather than anyone else?"

"There was a rumor going around that you were looking for the dog, and that you'd bring it once you found it. Smurov said something of the sort. We've all been trying to convince Ilusha the dog is alive, that it's been seen. The boys brought him a live hare; he just looked at it with a faint smile and asked them to let it go in the fields. So we did. His father just this minute got back, bringing him a mastiff pup, hoping to comfort him with that — but I think it only makes things worse."
"Tell me, Karamazov, what sort of man is the father? I know him, but what do you make of him — a mountebank, a buffoon?"

"Oh, no; there are people of deep feeling who've somehow been crushed. Buffoonery in people like that is a kind of resentful irony against those they don't dare tell the truth to, from years of being humiliated and intimidated by them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that sort of buffoonery is sometimes tragic in the extreme. His whole life now centers on Ilusha, and if Ilusha dies, he'll either go mad with grief or kill himself. I feel almost certain of that when I look at him now."
"I understand you, Karamazov. I can see you understand human nature," Kolya added, with feeling.
"And the moment I saw you with a dog, I thought you were bringing Zhutchka."

"Wait a bit, Karamazov, maybe we'll still find him yet; but this is Perezvon. I'll let him in now, and maybe it'll cheer Ilusha up more than the mastiff pup did. Wait a bit, Karamazov, you'll see something in a minute. But, I say, I'm keeping you standing here!" Kolya cried suddenly. "You've got no overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we're all egoists, Karamazov!"
"Don't worry about it — it's cold, but I don't catch cold easily. Let's go in, though, and, by the way, what's your name? I know you're called Kolya, but what else?"
"Nikolay — Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they say in official documents, 'son of Krassotkin.'" Kolya laughed for some reason, but then added suddenly, "Of course I hate my name, Nikolay."
"Why is that?"
"It's so trivial, so ordinary."
"You're thirteen?" Alyosha asked.

"No, fourteen — that is, I'll be fourteen very soon, in a fortnight. I'll confess one weakness of mine to you, Karamazov, just to you, since this is our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age — more than that ... and actually ... there's a slanderous story going around about me, that last week I was playing robbers with the preparatory boys. It's true I played with them, but it's a complete slander to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reason to believe you've heard the story; but I wasn't playing for my own amusement, it was for the children's sake, because they couldn't think up anything to do on their own. But they always have some silly tale going around. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you."
"But what if you had been playing for your own amusement — what's the harm in that?"
"Come now, my own amusement! You don't play horses, do you?"

"But you have to look at it this way," Alyosha said, smiling. "Grown-ups go to the theater, and there the adventures of all sorts of heroes are acted out — sometimes there are robbers and battles too — and isn't that just the same thing, in a different form, of course? And young people's games of soldiers or robbers in their free time are also art in its earliest stage. You know, they spring from the same growing artistic instincts in the young. And sometimes these games are much better than performances at the theater — the only difference is that people go there to watch actors, while in these games the young people are the actors themselves. But that's only natural."

"You think so? Is that your idea?" Kolya looked at him intently. "Oh, you know, that's actually a rather interesting way of looking at it. When I get home, I'll think it over. I'll admit I thought I might learn something from you. I've come to learn from you, Karamazov," Kolya concluded, in a voice full of unguarded feeling.
"And I from you," said Alyosha, smiling and pressing his hand.
Kolya was very pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly as an equal, talking to him just as though he were "fully grown up."
"I'll show you something in a minute, Karamazov — it's a bit of theater, too," he said, laughing nervously. "That's why I came."
"Let's go first to the landlord's, on the left. All the boys leave their coats there, since the room's small and hot."

"Oh, I'm only coming in for a minute. I'll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the hallway and play dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how dead he is. I'll go in first and scout around, then I'll whistle for him when I think it's time, and you'll see, he'll dash in like mad. Only Smurov mustn't forget to open the door at the right moment. I'll arrange it all — you'll see something."
